docs.title: orderflow-scaling
docs.text:
This project checks, pair by pair on about sixty cryptocurrencies, whether a single parameter — the persistence H0 of the signed order flow — fixes the roughness of volume, the exponent of market impact and the roughness of volatility, as predicted by Muhle-Karbe, Ouazzani Chahdi, Rosenbaum & Szymanski (2026).

Prediction Exponent H0 = 3/4 Signed flow H0 0.75 Volume rate H0 − 1/2 0.25 Extraday volatility 2H0 − 3/2 0 Impact (constant-rate meta-order, in time) 2 − 2H0 0.5

Result on the confirmation year (2025-11-01 to 2026-10-31; 60 spot pairs, 59 perpetuals; configuration frozen before that year was used). The gap is the observed exponent minus the prediction, averaged over pairs, with its 95 % interval. A relation is compatible when the joint test does not reject and the interval lies within ±0.05, rejected when the test rejects and the gap exceeds 0.05, undecided otherwise.

Prediction Spot Perpetual H1, volume roughness: H_vol = H0 − 1/2 rejected, gap −0.119 [−0.128, −0.099] compatible, gap +0.001 [−0.012, +0.011] H2, volatility roughness: H_σ = 2H0 − 3/2 rejected, gap +0.148 [+0.310, +0.565] rejected, gap +0.362 [+0.508, +0.782] H3, impact exponent, exploratory: δ = 2 − 2H0 rejected, gap −0.296 [−0.326, −0.275] † undecided, gap −0.384 [−0.401, −0.359] †

Where an interval does not contain its gap, most estimates of that exponent sit on the lower bound of their range, so their bootstrap is lopsided; the paper's reading aids count these cases.

† The control estimators find a gap that differs by more than 0.05: by the pre-registered rule this result does not count on its own.

Forecasting the average of the next 22 days (mean QLIKE ratio, below 1: the model forecasts better): F1, the rough predictor against HAR for volatility: 0.730 (undecided) on spot, 0.730 (undecided) on perpetuals; F2, the order-flow H against the measured H for volatility: 1.014 (undecided) on spot, 0.996 (equivalent) on perpetuals; F3, the rough predictor against HAR for volume: 0.889 (undecided) on spot, 0.880 (undecided) on perpetuals.

  • Architecture: six stages, one store, four outputs.
  • Data: Binance Vision formats and quality controls.
  • Estimators: what is estimated, how, and what simulation says about it.
  • Protocol: pre-registration, development and confirmation samples.
  • Operations: daily run, monitoring, incident procedures.
  • Compliance: every requirement of the specification, with its evidence.
  • Design decisions in ten questions: the choices a reviewer will question, answered.

Beyond the core tests:

  • Forecasting: does roughness forecast daily volatility and volume? An exact rough-volatility predictor against HAR, out of sample, with live daily forecasts.
  • Change-point monitor: CUSUM and Shiryaev–Roberts alarms when a pair's H0 leaves its development range.
  • L2 collector: local order books of the perpetuals from the WebSocket stream, sampled every second with every trade.
  • Other venues: the same H0 on the public trades of Bybit and OKX, to see how much the answer depends on the exchange (exploratory).

"Production grade" here means: one command rebuilds every result from scratch, the pipeline updates itself every day, every module has its tests, everything runs in a container and reports its own failures.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Idempotence: every output is named by (pair, day, version); re-running changes nothing, changing the version recomputes (ADR 0002).
  • Data contracts: every table has a pandera schema checked on write (ofs.schemas).
  • Research / production separation: notebooks explore, the package computes; no number of the report comes from a notebook.
  • Configuration outside the code: windows, grids, universe live in config/.

docs.title: Change-point monitor of H0 (extension)
docs.text:
The specification lists, among the extensions after the first version, "change-point detection on H: CUSUM or Shiryaev–Roberts on the rolling estimate of H, to spot a regime change of the flow" (§4). The theory treats H0 as a constant of each asset; this monitor says when that stops being true.

ofs changepoints --to 2026-10-31          # after the tag prereg-v1 (exploratory, like the rolling estimates)

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
1. Block estimates. The principal H0 estimator (mixed fBm on aggregated variances) is fitted on consecutive, non-overlapping blocks of 14 days. Daily features are additive, so a block estimate is one fit of the sum of its 14 daily rows; blocks with fewer than 10 observed days are left empty.
  2. Reference. The blocks of the development sample give the centre (median), the scale (1.4826 × MAD, robust to an outlying block) and the lag-1 autocorrelation φ of the block estimates (clipped to [0, 0.9]). Later blocks are standardised: z = (Ĥ0_block − median) / scale.
  3. Detectors, both two-sided and restarted after an alarm:
  4. CUSUM (Page, 1954): S⁺ = max(0, S⁺ + z − k), S⁻ = max(0, S⁻ − z − k), k = 0.5;
  5. Shiryaev–Roberts for a shift of ±1 reference sd: R = (1 + R) exp(±z − ½), computed in logs.
  6. Thresholds give an in-control average run length of 50 blocks (about two years). They are calibrated by simulation of a stationary AR(1) sequence with the reference φ: block estimates of a long-memory flow are positively correlated, and thresholds computed for independent blocks would raise false alarms much more often. The tests check the calibration on fresh simulations (within 15 %) and that a shift of 1.5 sds is caught in fewer than 8 blocks on average.

Settings live in config/pipeline.yaml (monitoring.changepoint): monitoring choices, outside the frozen estimation configuration and outside the confirmatory tests.

docs.title: Where it shows
docs.text:
• data/monitoring/changepoints.parquet: one row per pair, market and block after the reference, with the estimate, z, both statistics, the thresholds and the alarms;
  • the daily run updates it once a week and lists the pairs with an alarm in the latest block in its status (changepoint_alarms), without failing the run;
  • GET /monitor/changepoints?symbol=BTCUSDT&alarms_only=true;
  • dashboard, asset sheet: "Regime monitor of H0" (block estimates, reference band, alarms).

docs.title: Reading an alarm
docs.text: An alarm says that the order-flow persistence of the pair left its development range, not why: a change in the mix of participants, a fee or tick change, a listing on another venue, a structural event (stablecoin de-peg, delisting threat). For the tests of the scaling laws, a pair with an alarm inside the confirmation sample is a candidate for the robustness variant "without regime changes"; the confirmatory tests themselves are not changed by the monitor.

docs.title: Data sources: survey and choice
docs.text: Survey made on 2026-11-09, before the real-data collection. It answers one question: which public source gives the best trade-level data for the tests, for free and reproducibly?

docs.title: OKX archive (for the extension)
docs.text:
Checked on the real files:

  • https://www.okx.com/cdn/okex/traderecords/trades/daily/{YYYYMMDD}/{INSTRUMENT}-trades-{YYYY-MM-DD}.zip, with INSTRUMENT BTC-USDT (spot) or BTC-USDT-SWAP (linear perpetual); columns instrument_name, trade_id, side, price, size, created_time (ms), source.

docs.title: Quality controls (blocking)
docs.text:
• SHA-256 equal to .CHECKSUM, else one new download, then checksum_failed.
  • Schema (pandera), non-empty file, strictly increasing agg_trade_id.
  • Trade-id continuity last_i + 1 = first_{i+1} and consecutive agg_trade_id: every gap is logged. USD-M files miss short runs of trade ids that are never published (0.01 % of the ids in early 2025, 0.1-0.3 % from mid-2025; spot: none), while their aggTrade ids stay consecutive. A day is blocked when aggTrade rows are missing, when one run of more than 1000 trade ids is missing, or when more than 2 % of the ids are (ADR 0012).
  • Positive prices and quantities; timestamps sorted and inside the UTC day.
  • OHLC rebuilt from aggTrades against the 1-minute klines: no minute missing, none off by more than 1 %, at most 0.5 % of minutes off by more than max(0.01 %, 2 ticks) (ADR 0009: USD-M klines contain a few trades absent from aggTrades and may open at the previous minute's last price; spot matches exactly).
  • Price moves above 20 % within one second: flagged for inspection, not blocking.
  • Files re-published by Binance: there is no separate updates folder on Binance Vision (checked on 2026-11-09: the bucket holds data/, a legacy archive data2/ and liquidation snapshots data3/); a corrected file replaces the old one at the same URL with a new .CHECKSUM. ofs recheck compares the published checksums with the manifest and, for every changed day, downloads, validates and reduces it again, then recomputes pass 2 of the neighbouring days (ADR 0010). The daily run does it every week over the last 30 days.

docs.title: Universe
docs.text:
ofs universe lists the USDT spot pairs (S3 listing), removes stablecoin/stablecoin, fiat and leveraged tokens, ranks by median daily quote volume over 24 months and keeps the first 60 with ≥ 95 % days available; it attaches the USD-M perpetual (also with the 1000… prefixes) and merges renamed symbols via config/symbol_renames.yaml. Availability is counted on the daily aggTrades files of the S3 listing, for the spot pair and for the perpetual, because klines can outlive trades: the RAYUSDT perpetual has 1-minute klines through 2026 but no aggTrades after 2022-11-15, so it is not attached. The file is written as a draft; review the rename table, then rerun with --freeze.

Renames

config/symbol_renames.yaml lists MATIC→POL, RNDR→RENDER and FTM→S per market. The dates were checked on the S3 listing (last daily file of the old symbol, first daily file of the new one). The perpetual stopped trading before the spot pair each time, and the few days of the token swap have no file on either symbol: these days are recorded as suspended (explained gaps), not missing. An unknown rename splits a pair into two partial series, each below 95 % coverage: the pair is then excluded (conservative, never wrong data).

docs.title: Deploying on Oracle Cloud
docs.text: The whole stack of docker-compose.yml (daily pipeline, API, dashboard and the HTTPS proxy) runs on one Arm virtual machine of Oracle Cloud's "Always Free" tier. Within the free limits it costs nothing. Check Oracle's current limits and rules first: the figures below are those of the time of writing.

docs.text: The free Arm machines exist only in the account's home region, chosen at sign-up and fixed afterwards. Choose a region outside the United States: Binance refuses US addresses on its live API, which the optional L2 collector uses.

docs.title: 3. Ports
docs.text:
Two firewalls must let HTTP and HTTPS in:

  1. The cloud network: Networking, Virtual cloud networks, the network of the machine, Security lists, the default list, Add ingress rules: source 0.0.0.0/0, protocol TCP, destination ports 80,443.
  2. The machine itself: Oracle's Ubuntu images reject everything but SSH in iptables; scripts/vm-setup.sh (step 5) adds the two rules and saves them.

docs.title: 4. Hostnames
docs.text:
Caddy serves the API and the dashboard on two names that point to the machine's public address, and obtains their certificates by itself. Either:

  • a free DuckDNS name (duckdns.org): create yourname and enter the address; the sub-names api.yourname.duckdns.org and dashboard.yourname.duckdns.org resolve to the same address;
  • or a domain of your own, with two A records.

docs.title: 5. Code and set-up
docs.text:
ssh ubuntu@<public-address>
git clone https://github.com/NIDHAL277/orderflow-scaling && cd orderflow-scaling
bash scripts/vm-setup.sh
exit            # log in again once, so that docker works without sudo

Before the repository is public, bring the code as a git bundle instead of cloning: git bundle create ofs.bundle main --tags on the laptop, scp ofs.bundle ubuntu@<public-address>:, then git clone ofs.bundle orderflow-scaling on the machine.

In .env, set OFS_API_HOST and OFS_DASHBOARD_HOST to the two names; optionally the Healthchecks.io URL and the Cloudflare R2 keys of the weekly backup.

docs.title: 6. Data
docs.text:
The daily run continues from the derived tables, the same as those of the weekly backup (scripts/backup.sh): about 4 GB (3.8 GB in November 2026), mostly daily statistics, then the comparison of venues and the validation records. The dashboard also needs quality, monitoring and venues (data quality, regime monitor, comparison of venues): without them those sections stay empty. The raw Binance files are never copied: the pipeline downloads what it needs. From the laptop, in the repository (ofs compact first folds the closed months into one file per statistic, pair and month: about 280,000 files to copy instead of more than a million):

uv run ofs compact
cd data
tar czf - daily_stats estimates tests forecast manifest validation simulation status cache \
    quality monitoring venues \
  | ssh ubuntu@<public-address> "tar xzf - -C orderflow-scaling/data"
ssh ubuntu@<public-address> "sudo chown -R 1000:1000 orderflow-scaling/data"

On a slow or unstable connection, a dropped stream starts the copy again from zero. Send it in parts instead, so that a dropped connection costs one part (copy again any part whose check fails):

tar cf - daily_stats estimates tests forecast manifest validation simulation status cache \
    quality monitoring venues | split -b 256M -d -a 3 - ofs-data.tar.part-
sha256sum ofs-data.tar.part-* > SHA256SUMS
ssh ubuntu@<public-address> "mkdir -p ofs-parts"
scp ofs-data.tar.part-* SHA256SUMS ubuntu@<public-address>:ofs-parts/
ssh ubuntu@<public-address> "cd ofs-parts && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS \
  && cat ofs-data.tar.part-* | tar xf - -C ../orderflow-scaling/data \
  && sudo chown -R 1000:1000 ../orderflow-scaling/data"

docs.title: 7. Start
docs.text:
Once a release is tagged (v1.0.0, say), the release workflow publishes the image on GHCR for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. A new GHCR package can start private: make it public in its package settings on GitHub, or run docker login ghcr.io on the machine. Then:

docker compose pull && docker compose up -d

Before that, build it on the machine instead: docker compose build && docker compose up -d.

Checks:

docker compose ps                          # pipeline, api, dashboard, caddy: running
docker compose exec pipeline ofs status
curl -s https://api.yourname.duckdns.org/health

The dashboard is then at https://dashboard.yourname.duckdns.org.

docs.title: 8. Keep it running
docs.text:
• Healthchecks.io alerts by email when the daily ping does not arrive.
  • Updates: git pull && docker compose pull && docker compose up -d.
  • Oracle may reclaim an Always Free machine that stays idle for seven days (low use of processor, network and memory). At the time of writing, upgrading the account to "Pay As You Go" lifts that rule while the Always Free resources stay free; a budget alert of 1 € then warns of any charge.

docs.title: Design decisions in twelve questions
docs.text: The choices a reviewer is most likely to question, each with the short answer, the evidence, and where it lives in the code.

docs.title: 1. Why test the theory asset by asset rather than on average?
docs.text: The theory predicts relations between exponents (H_vol = H0 − 1/2, H_σ = 2H0 − 3/2, δ = 2 − 2H0). An average over assets can match the prediction by coincidence; a relation must also hold across assets whose H0 differ. So each pair gives a point (Ĥ0, Ŷ), and the test is on the line through 60 points: slope and intercept jointly, against the predicted ones. Both coordinates are estimated with error, so ordinary least squares would flatten the slope (attenuation bias); Deming regression uses the ratio of the two error variances, taken from the bootstrap. The risk is low power if H0 hardly varies across pairs; the decision rule then says "undecided" rather than forcing an answer. Code: ofs.inference.hypotheses.cross_test, ofs.inference.deming.

docs.title: 2. How is H0 estimated, and why weights ∝ 1/τ?
docs.text:
The signed flow is modelled as a fractional part plus a martingale (the paper's Theorem 3.6): Var(X_{t+τ} − X_t) = σ1² τ^{2H0} + σ2² τ. The aggregated variance V(τ) is fitted by weighted non-linear least squares over τ from 10 s to 4 h. The sampling variance of log V(τ) grows roughly like τ, so weights ∝ 1/τ are the inverse-variance weights; in simulation they halve the standard deviation compared with equal weights and remove a spurious H on Brownian data. If the fractional part is not significant at 4 h, H0 is set to 1/2. Code: ofs.estimators.h0, ADR 0008.

Why is the flow centred day by day in proportion to volume? Because the development year showed that otherwise a day-level imbalance reads as memory. * What failed. The negative control (signs shuffled within each day) gave 0.80 instead of 0.5. The shuffle keeps each day's net buying or selling, which rides on bursts of activity, and the control had removed a drift uniform in time. * How far it goes. Without centring, memoryless signs with a 5 % daily imbalance read as H0 ≈ 0.98 in simulation. * The fix. Each 10-second window now loses its volume times the day's imbalance. Removing a day's net increment shrinks the variance at large τ like a bridge, and the fit uses that exact shape, so genuine memory is not biased. * The result. The shuffled control returns 0.49–0.50, and real H0 drops by about 0.03. * Why simulation missed it. The simulated trades arrived uniformly in time; real activity clusters. * It was decided on development data before the confirmation year was touched, and is logged as deviations D3/D4 (ADR 0015).

docs.title: 3. Why reduce the trades to additive daily statistics?
docs.text: Every estimator is written as fit(sum of daily feature rows): sums of squared increments per lag, counts, cross-products. Then a bootstrap replicate is just a weight vector over days, the 999 replicates of 120 pair-markets never re-read a trade, raw files can be deleted after reduction (the 24 months would not fit otherwise), and a block of 14 days for the change-point monitor is one fit of 14 summed rows. Code: ofs.reduce, ofs.estimators.base.Features, ADR 0004.

docs.title: 4. Why a synchronized block bootstrap, and why widen it by k?
docs.text: Days are resampled by blocks (stationary bootstrap, mean 7 days) because one-day blocks would destroy the long memory being measured; the same resampled days are applied to every pair, because crypto pairs move together and the cross-sectional test must see that correlation. Under long memory, the block bootstrap still underestimates the sampling spread on one-year samples; the full simulation measured the ratio of true to bootstrap standard deviation, and its median over the principal estimators' plausible cells widens every interval: 1.14 at registration, 1.06 since the volume-centred H0 (deviation D4), whose intervals are better calibrated. Code: ofs.inference.bootstrap, ofs.simulate.decisions.

docs.title: 5. Why simulate before touching real data, and what did it change?
docs.text: Every estimator is biased somewhere; the only way to know where is to run it on data with a known answer, through the same reduction code. The full study (82 cells × 200 replications of 365 days) changed three choices: the paper's autocovariance GMM replaced the moments for H_vol (moments biased up to 0.079 by noise); the quadratic-variation ratio replaced the sign autocorrelation as control of H0 (biased by 0.033); and it showed that H_σ near 0.1 cannot be estimated within 0.02 on one year. The rules that turned these numbers into decisions were written before the study ran. Code: ofs.simulate.study, pre-registration §4.1.

docs.title: 6. Why Whittle for H_σ, and why is H2 "limited"?
docs.text: Daily realised variance is a day average of volatility plus measurement error. The Whittle estimator of Fukasawa, Takabatake & Westphal models exactly that (day-averaged fBm plus white noise) and stays consistent near H = 0; the GJR moment regression ignores the averaging and is biased upward near 0 (+0.121 in the study). Whittle still misses the 0.02 tolerance (0.030), so H2 is reported as limited by estimator reliability. The rule's fallback kept GJR; deviation D1 made Whittle principal, before any real-data estimate (config/deviations.md). The theory puts H_σ near 0 to 0.1, exactly where estimation is hardest: that is a finding, not a failure.

docs.title: 7. Why "rejected / compatible / undecided" with a margin?
docs.text: With enough data any tiny deviation is significant, and absence of significance is not evidence of agreement. So a relation is rejected only if the Holm-corrected Wald test rejects at 1 % and the mean gap exceeds 0.05 (Hurst units); compatible only if the test does not reject and the 95 % interval of the gap lies within ±0.05 (an equivalence test); otherwise undecided, with the number of days that would decide. The same rule decides the forecasting hypotheses with a 2 % margin on the loss ratio. Code: ofs.inference.hypotheses.decide.

docs.title: 8. Why a pre-registration enforced in code?
docs.text: With four exponents, several estimators, windows, τ ranges and samples, there are hundreds of ways to get a "significant" result. Writing the hypotheses, estimators and decision rules down and tagging them (prereg-v1) before any real-data estimate, then freezing the configuration (config-frozen) before the confirmation sample, removes that freedom. The code refuses to estimate before the tags and checks that the configuration is unchanged; in the container, CI bakes the tag list and the config hash into the image. Every later change is a dated deviation. Code: ofs.protocol, ADR 0006.

docs.title: 9. Why an "exact" rough predictor, QLIKE, and a lognormal level correction?
docs.text: The published rough-volatility forecast (Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum, 2018) assumes a continuously observed, noise-free fBm; daily RV is a noisy day average. Conditioning a Gaussian model of exactly that (the Whittle model) gives the optimal linear forecast; in simulation the published kernel lost 13 % of one-step MSE to it. QLIKE and MSE on levels rank forecasts correctly even with a noisy RV proxy (Patton, 2011), which the MSE of logs does not. Each log model returns to levels with its own lognormal correction: the empirical smearing factor was too noisy at 22 days and changed rankings. Result in simulation: about 1 % better than HAR at one day, 7–13 % at 22 days. Code: ofs.forecast, ADR 0013.

docs.title: 10. What broke on real data, and what changed because of it?
docs.text:
• USD-M trade ids go missing (0.1–0.3 % from mid-2025) while aggregate ids stay consecutive: continuity is checked on aggregate ids, trade-id gaps by fraction and run length (ADR 0012).
  • Futures klines may open at the previous close: the OHLC check accepts either (ADR 0009).
  • Binance re-publishes corrected files at the same URL: a weekly checksum recheck (ADR 0010).
  • Perpetuals keep publishing flat klines after trading stops; klines outlive trades: days without trades are dropped and availability is counted on the trade listing.
  • The USD-M WebSocket serves trades only on /market (the root accepts the subscription and sends nothing): the collector uses two connections (ADR 0014).
  • Operations: a shell filter deleted derived data, a closed lid killed the jobs, a restart stopped them again. Hence explicit-name cleanup only, resumable jobs, and a resume script (incident notes in docs/incidents/).
  • Small files: on the laptop's hard disk the daily cycle of 2026-11-15 took 11 hours, nearly all of it opening about 955,000 files of a few kilobytes. Closed months are now folded into one file per statistic, pair and month, read back and compared before the daily files go (ADR 0016); the bundles read from both layouts were identical on real data.
  • The health check said "ok" with data 16 days old: it now reports "stale" once the last verified day is more than 3 days old.

docs.title: 11. What did the confirmation year show?
docs.text:
Every choice was frozen on 2026-11-14 (tag config-frozen) before the confirmation year (2025-11-01 to 2026-10-31) was estimated.

  • Volume (H1): compatible on perpetuals (gap +0.001, interval −0.012 to +0.011), rejected on spot (−0.119).
  • Volatility (H2): rejected on both markets. With H0 below 3/4 the relation predicts a negative H_σ, which no Hurst exponent can take; the daily estimates sit on the lower bound of their range, so the intervals are lopsided.
  • Impact (H3, exploratory): rejected on spot; undecided on perpetuals, where the gap is large (−0.384) but H0 spans only 0.54 to 0.62 across pairs, too narrow to identify a slope. The control estimators disagree on the size of the gap, so H3 never counts alone.
  • Level of H0 (H4): 0.700 on spot and 0.597 on perpetuals (development: 0.705, 0.590).
  • Forecasts (F1–F3): at 22 days the rough predictor's loss is 27 % below HAR's for volatility, but the interval is wide and the Holm-corrected test does not decide. Using the order-flow H instead of the measured one changes forecasts by less than 1.5 %: equivalent at 1 and 5 days.

Five of the six primary decisions of the development year were reproduced. The one change, H3 on perpetuals (rejected, then undecided), comes from the narrow cross-section, not from a change of method. Numbers: the README (generated from the result tables) and paper/main.pdf.

docs.title: 12. What are the limits, and what would come next?
docs.text:
• One main venue. Bybit and OKX are an exploratory check on five pairs over one month: on perpetuals they agree with Binance within 0.03 on average (docs/venues.md).
  • H_σ near zero is where the estimators are least reliable (Whittle's bias 0.030 in the simulation study). H2's rejection rests on the sign of the predicted exponent more than on the precision of the estimate.
  • δ uses a proxy of price impact built from trades; there is no order-book history (the L2 collector starts one).
  • One year per sample, and the live track record of the forecasts has only just started.
  • Next: run the daily pipeline on a server to build that live record, extend the venue comparison, and re-run the same frozen protocol on the following year as a second confirmation.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text: Every estimator is a pure function of daily sufficient statistics, split into features(stats, days) (a days × K matrix of additive daily features) and fit(sums) (ADR 0004). Roles (principal, control, robustness, diagnostic, negative control) are assigned in ofs.estimators.registry from config/estimation.yaml.

docs.title: H0 — signed flow
docs.text:
X is the cumulative deseasonalised signed notional on windows of Δ, centred day by day in proportion to volume (ADR 0015, deviation D4). Each window loses m_d V, its volume times the day's imbalance m_d = net flow / volume. A day-level imbalance riding on bursts of activity is then not read as memory; the uncentred flow reads a memoryless 5 % daily imbalance as H0 ≈ 0.98.

  • Principal — mixed fBm (mixed_fbm_vc): E[(X_{t+τ} − X_t)²] = σ1² τ^{2H0} + σ2² τ.
  • Fitted by weighted NLS on log-variances, with weights ∝ 1/τ (inverse variance under the Brownian null), for τ from Δ to 4 h.
  • Both terms take their exact expected shape after the daily centring, a bridge: g_H(m) = m^{2H} − 2(m/N)A(m) + (m/N)² N^{2H}.
  • The fractional component must explain, at 4 h, more than twice the sampling error of the variance there (2·sqrt(4m/3n), floor 5 %). Otherwise the flow is Brownian and H0 = 1/2 (ADR 0008).
  • Control — quadratic-variation ratio on (Δ, 2Δ, 4Δ), the paper's own estimator H = ½ log2[(V(4Δ) − 2V(2Δ)) / (V(2Δ) − 2V(Δ))], on the same flow. The simulation study chose it over the sign autocorrelation, which was biased by 0.033.
  • Robustness:
  • the other windows Δ;
  • no deseasonalisation;
  • τ up to 1 h;
  • uncentred, the pre-registered principal on the uncentred flow.
  • Diagnostics:
  • the simple fBm slope, which reproduces the paper's bias rising with Δ;
  • DFA-2;
  • the event-time sign autocorrelation, C(ℓ) ~ ℓ^{−γ}, H0 = 1 − γ/2, fitted on the leading run of lag bins significantly above zero.
  • Negative control: signs permuted within each day, then the same centring and fit; it must give 1/2 (deviation D3). The shuffled sign autocorrelation is no control: its flat autocorrelation gives H0 = 1 by construction.

docs.title: H_vol — volume rate
docs.text: v_k = V_k / Δ, deseasonalised. Principal: moments m(q, ℓ) = mean|v_{k+ℓ} − v_k|^q ~ ℓ^{q H} with a linearity check of ζ(q). Control: the same on log v. Also computed: the paper's autocovariance-GMM of increments truncated at 3 sd, which models white observation noise explicitly.

docs.title: H_σ — volatility
docs.text:
The theory predicts the extraday roughness (paper, Remark 4.2): daily horizon primary.

  • GJR moments of log σ increments on daily 5-minute RV (lags 1–50 days); TSRV variant.
  • Whittle (Fukasawa, Takabatake & Westphal): increments of log RV modelled as increments of a day-averaged fBm plus white measurement noise, spectral density f(λ) = ν²[4 c_H (1 − cos λ)² Σ_k |λ + 2πk|^{−2H−3} + r (1 − cos λ)/π]; its bootstrap re-estimates on block-resampled series without cross-block increments.
  • p-variation (Cont & Das): H = 1/p* where the p-variation stops depending on the step.
  • Intraday horizon (15-minute local variances of 10-second returns): descriptive.
  • Long history (spec §4): the same daily estimators on up to 5 years of daily RV rebuilt from monthly 1-minute klines (ofs history, sample history, variant daily_5y); a robustness variant of H2 (ADR 0011).

docs.title: δ — impact
docs.text: Proxy A: runs of same-sign trades less than g seconds apart, I = ε (log p_last − log p_first), fit E[I | Q] = A Q^δ on log-binned notional (control: on run duration). Proxy B: aggregate impact against the normalised imbalance (descriptive).

docs.title: What the simulations say
docs.text:
Quick profile (ofs simulate study --profile quick, 2026-11-09: 40 replications per cell, 99 bootstrap draws, 20 simulated days, 120 for H_σ):

Exponent Finding Consequence H0 mixed fBm (1/τ weights): |bias| ≤ 0.02 in all 20 cells (H0 0.6-0.9, noise/signal 0-2) principal kept H0 equal weights in log space: same bias, twice the sd; spurious H on Brownian data weights 1/τ (ADR 0008) H0 sign ACF on Lillo-Mike-Farmer signs: biased low for H0 ≥ 0.75 (finite-size effect of the model) control choice ruled in the pre-registration H_vol moments and log-moments biased by observation noise; autocovariance-GMM unbiased up to noise/signal 1 rule in the pre-registration §4.1 H_σ GJR on daily RV biased up by ≈ 0.1 everywhere; Whittle much closer on 365 days rule in the pre-registration §4.1 δ proxy A unbiased — all 95 % bootstrap CIs too narrow on short samples: H0 coverage 72 % (20 days), 78 % (60), 85 % (120) pre-registered calibration sd_inflation from the full study

The coverage problem is the known weakness of block bootstraps under long memory: the bootstrap spread approaches the true one as the sample grows (true sd / bootstrap sd 1.48 at 20 days, 1.13 at 120), and longer blocks do not help (1.38 with 30-day blocks at 120 days: fewer blocks make the bootstrap itself noisier). The full profile therefore simulates 365-day samples, like the real ones, and reports sd_ratio per cell.

docs.title: Full profile (2026-11-10): the pre-registered decisions
docs.text:
82 cells, 200 replications of 365 days, 199 bootstrap draws (ofs simulate decide --profile full; worst |bias| over the cells of the plausible region, noise/signal ≤ 1):

Exponent Candidates (worst |bias|) Decision H0 mixed fBm 0.001 principal H0 control sign ACF 0.033, quadratic-variation ratio 0.000 QV ratio replaces the sign ACF H_vol autocovariance GMM 0.014, moments 0.079 GMM principal, moments control H_σ GJR 0.121, Whittle 0.030 (H_σ ∈ [0.05, 0.15]) neither within 0.02: the rule kept GJR; deviation D1 makes Whittle principal; H2 reported as limited δ proxy A 0.000 principal calibration median true sd / bootstrap sd over 39 cells k = 1.14 at registration (H0 coverage 72-94 % raw, 80-96 % with k); k = 1.06 after the volume-centred H0 of D4 (H0 bias 0.0005, coverage 89-96 % raw, 91.5-98 % with k)

Controls that fail the bias rule (moments for H_vol, GJR for H_σ) are reported but do not decide whether a result counts (deviation D2, config/deviations.md).

The H_σ result is itself a finding: on one year of daily data, roughness near H = 0.1 cannot be estimated within 0.02 by either estimator; the five-year history variant (daily_5y) of the specification curve shows how much a longer sample helps.

The definitive tables come from make sim (profile full) and are part of the report.

docs.title: Forecasting extension (F)
docs.text:
The scaling laws say how rough volatility should be, H_σ = 2 H0 − 3/2 (paper, Remark 4.2). The forecasting extension asks the practical question: does that roughness help forecast volatility, and does the roughness implied by order flow forecast as well as the roughness measured on volatility itself? Daily traded volume gets the same treatment.

It is a statistical evaluation (losses, Diebold–Mariano tests, model confidence set). The specification excludes trading strategies and P&L backtests (§4), and so does this extension. The design is pre-registered (config/preregistration.md §10) and frozen with the rest of config/estimation.yaml.

ofs forecast --sample development --jobs 4      # needs the tag prereg-v1
ofs forecast --sample confirmation --jobs 4     # needs config-frozen (confirmatory)
ofs simulate forecast --reps 10 --jobs 4        # check on simulated rough volatility

docs.title: Target, data, origins
docs.text:
• Target: the average of the series over the next h days, y_h(t) = mean(y[t+1..t+h]), h ∈ {1, 5, 22} (day, week, month; Corsi, 2009). Series: daily 5-minute realised variance (rv_5m) and daily traded quote volume (quote_volume).
  • Data: the 5-year daily history from monthly 1-minute klines (daily_stats/rv_history, ADR 0011), cut at the end of the evaluated sample: no later day is read.
  • Origins: every day of the evaluated period. development: 2023-05-01 → 2025-10-31 (the first origin needs a 500-day window); confirmation: 2025-11-01 → 2026-10-31. Forecasts use the data up to and including the origin only; a test perturbs every value after the origin and checks that no forecast moves.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Model Forecast of the log series Parameters (rolling 500-day window) rw last value none ar_log AR(5) on log y, direct projection on log y_h OLS, refitted daily har HAR of Corsi (2009) on levels OLS, insanity filter (in-window range) har_log HAR on the logs of the daily, weekly, monthly averages (benchmark) OLS rough_gjr kernel of Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum (2018, §5) as published H by their moment regression rough_rolling exact predictor (below) H, noise ratio, scale by Whittle rough_dev exact predictor H = development estimate of H_σ; noise ratio by Whittle rough_theory exact predictor H = 2 Ĥ0 − 3/2 (development H0, floored at 0.01)

Rough parameters are re-estimated every 5 days, regressions every day.

docs.title: The exact rough predictor
docs.text:
The daily log RV is modelled as the Whittle estimator of Fukasawa, Takabatake & Westphal already models it for H_σ: the day average of a fractional Brownian motion plus white measurement noise, Y_t = c + ν · mean_{day t} W^H + ε_t. Its increments are stationary with autocovariance ν² [g_H(k) + r (2·1{k=0} − 1{|k|=1})], where r = var ε / ν² and

g_H(k) = ½ δ⁴Φ(k),   Φ(x) = |x|^{2H+2} / ((2H+1)(2H+2))      (fourth central difference)

is the autocovariance of the increments of day-averaged fBm (a test checks it against the spectral density the Whittle estimator uses, to 6 digits). The forecast of Y_{t+D} is the Gaussian conditional expectation given the last 499 increments: one Toeplitz system per horizon (Levinson recursion), weights on past values summing to one (no level parameter). The same algebra gives the prediction-error variance, hence the level forecast E[e^{Y_{t+D}}] = exp(forecast + ½ var). A test checks on simulated paths that the one-step mean squared error equals that variance.

docs.title: Why not just the published kernel
docs.text: The GJR (2018) formula is the prediction of a continuously observed, noise-free fBm with an infinite past. Daily RV is neither: it is a daily average and it carries estimation noise. In a probe on simulated fBm sampled daily (H = 0.1, 200-day window), the one-step mean squared error of the kernel discretised by cell integrals was 13 % above that of the exact Gaussian predictor (midpoint cells: 5 %); the kernel puts 63 % of the weight on the last day. With measurement noise the gap widens. rough_gjr is kept as the published benchmark, rough_rolling is the principal rough model.

docs.title: From log forecasts to levels
docs.text: Every log model maps its forecast to a level with its own lognormal correction exp(μ + s²/2): in-window residual variance (regressions), model-implied conditional variance (exact predictor), c_H K D^{2H} with c_H = Γ(3/2−H) / (Γ(H+1/2) Γ(2−2H)) (GJR kernel). The empirical smearing factor of Duan (1983) is available (level_correction: smearing) but is noisy at long horizons: 250 overlapping 22-day ratios hold about 11 independent blocks. With the true parameters, smearing cost the exact predictor about 10 % of QLIKE at 22 days in the probe, the lognormal correction 0.5 %.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
• Losses on the level of the target: QLIKE y/f − log(y/f) − 1 (primary) and squared error. With a noisy but conditionally unbiased proxy (daily RV for integrated variance) both rank forecasts as the latent variance would (Patton, 2011); the squared error of logs does not and is not used.
  • Per pair: mean losses on the dates where every model forecasts, ratio to har_log, Diebold–Mariano test against har_log (Newey–West with max(h−1, ⌊4(T/100)^{2/9}⌋) lags, Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold correction, Student t), model confidence set of Hansen, Lunde & Nason (2011) at 90 % (T_max statistic, stationary bootstrap of dates, mean block 22 days).
  • Pooled across pairs (hypotheses): per pair the loss differential is scaled by the mean loss of the reference model, averaged across the pairs present each date, and the DM test is run on that single series (cross-sectional correlation between cryptos is then harmless). Its mean is the average relative change of the loss, ratio − 1, with a stationary-bootstrap 95 % CI over dates.
  • Decision rule: the one of the main tests, on the relative loss change, with margin 0.02: better / worse when the Holm-corrected DM test rejects at 1 % and |ratio − 1| > 0.02; equivalent when it does not reject and the CI lies within [0.98, 1.02]; undecided otherwise.
Hypothesis Target Model / reference Reading F1 volatility rough_rolling / har_log does roughness forecast better than HAR? F2 volatility rough_theory / rough_dev does the order-flow H forecast as well as the volatility H? The theory passes if equivalent F3 volume rough_rolling / har_log F1 for traded volume

On the development sample rough_dev and rough_theory take H from estimates of the same period: their rows are flagged look_ahead and are exploratory. On the confirmation sample H comes from the development sample only, so F2 is a genuine out-of-sample test of the scaling law.

docs.title: Simulation check
docs.text:
ofs simulate forecast simulates the model of the exact predictor (H ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, noise sd ∈ {0, 0.3}, ν = 0.3, 1,500 days) and reports each model's QLIKE relative to har_log (data/simulation/forecast_study.parquet, report table tab:forecast-sim).

Full run (2026-11-10, 10 replications per cell; mean ratio to har_log, with the range over the six (H, noise) cells):

Model h = 1 h = 5 h = 22 rough_rolling (H by Whittle on the window) 0.988-0.992 0.960-0.979 0.873-0.932 rough_dev (true H) 0.986-0.989 0.946-0.974 0.860-0.927 rough_gjr (published kernel) 0.995-1.083 0.983-1.083 0.901-0.999 ar_log 1.003-1.015 0.996-1.030 0.968-1.037 har (levels) 1.008-1.609 1.015-2.307 1.015-1.680 rw 1.08-1.61 1.27-2.65 1.55-3.87

The exact predictor beats HAR in 90-100 % of the replications at one day and in 70-90 % at 22 days; the Whittle H of the window is close to the truth (0.105 for 0.1, 0.215 for 0.2; 0.10 for 0.05 with noise, where roughness and noise are hardest to separate). The published kernel loses to HAR at short horizons once there is measurement noise (+8 % at H = 0.05) but helps at 22 days. HAR on levels is unstable at H = 0.2 (ratios up to 2.3 with a large spread): heavy-tailed levels defeat the insanity filter, which is why the logs version is the benchmark.

Earlier exploratory run (4 replications, H = 0.1, noise 0.3):

Model h = 1 h = 5 h = 22 rough_rolling 0.989 0.976 0.915 rough_dev (true H) 0.988 0.975 0.915 rough_gjr 1.030 1.053 0.981 ar_log 1.019 1.055 1.084 har (levels) 1.028 1.055 1.053 rw 1.40 2.10 2.88

Under rough volatility the exact predictor wins and its advantage grows with the horizon; estimating H costs nothing against knowing it (Whittle underestimates H and the noise ratio together on 500-day windows, with little effect on the forecasts). A weekly CI test (tests/simulation/test_forecast_sim.py, marked slow) keeps these orderings.

docs.title: Live forecasts (production)
docs.text: The daily run (ofs daily) also forecasts every pair at the end of the day just completed, with every configured model, for the next 1, 5 and 22 days (ofs.forecast.live). The series is the 5-year history (complete months, klines) followed by the daily aggTrades statistics for the days it does not cover yet: the same 5-minute RV, and the notional traded as the quote volume. Each day's forecasts are written once (data/forecast/live/{day}.parquet) and never recomputed; as targets complete, the run scores them (live_scored.parquet), which builds a live, genuinely out-of-sample track record of every model. GET /forecast/live serves the latest forecasts (with the annualised volatility sqrt(365 × average daily variance)); the dashboard shows them as a "live outlook" with the track record. Live forecasts estimate on real data, so they start once the protocol allows the rolling estimates (tag prereg-v1).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: data/forecast/: forecasts_{sample}.parquet (one row per pair, market, target, model, horizon and origin, with the realised target, both losses, H and the noise ratio), evaluation_{sample}.parquet (per pair) and tests_{sample}.parquet (F1–F3). They are served by the API (/forecast/tests, /forecast/evaluation, /forecasts/{symbol}, /forecast/live), shown on the dashboard page Forecasting, and in the report (table tab:forecast, figure 9).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The rough predictor assumes the H of the window holds over the horizon; regime changes are not modelled by the forecasts (the change-point monitor of H0, changepoints, flags them separately).
  • No weekday effect is modelled for any model (weekends trade less in crypto).
  • rough_theory floors 2 Ĥ0 − 3/2 at 0.01: for Ĥ0 < 0.755 the theory predicts a non-positive H_σ, which no fBm predictor can use; the number of floored pairs is reported.

docs.title: L2 collector for the perpetuals (extension)
docs.text:
The free daily files carry trades and klines, not the order book. The specification lists as an extension "L2 data of the perpetuals: a continuous WebSocket collector, for a true propagator model" (§4). ofs collect-l2 is that collector.

ofs collect-l2 --symbol BTCUSDT --symbol ETHUSDT --symbol SOLUSDT --levels 20 --interval-ms 1000
docker compose --profile l2 up -d collector          # on the VM, always on

docs.title: What it records
docs.text:
Under data/l2/um/{SYMBOL}/{YYYY-MM-DD}/, one file per UTC hour and kind:

File Rows Columns {HH}_book.parquet one per interval_ms while the book is synchronised ts_ms, best bid/ask, mid, spread_bps, microprice, imbalance_1, depth within 10 bps of the mid on each side, the top levels levels (bid_px_i, bid_qty_i, ask_px_i, ask_qty_i), last_update_id, book_event_ms {HH}_trades.parquet every aggregated trade ts_ms (trade time), agg_trade_id, price, quantity, first/last trade id, is_buyer_maker, event_ms

A restart within an hour writes {HH}_{kind}_part{n}.parquet (never an overwrite); every write is atomic. Three perpetuals at 1 s and 20 levels take about 15 MB a day.

docs.title: How the book is kept right
docs.text:
Binance's rules for a local USD-M book (ofs.collect.book.BookSync):

  1. buffer the diff-depth events, take a REST snapshot (lastUpdateId = L);
  2. drop events with u < L; the first applied event must bridge the snapshot, U ≤ L ≤ u;
  3. afterwards every event's pu must equal the previous u; otherwise the book is lost and rebuilt from a new snapshot (counted as a resync);
  4. sizes are absolute; zero removes a level; removing an absent level is normal.

A crossed book (best bid ≥ best ask) is also rebuilt. Books are sampled only while synchronised, and are reset the moment the depth connection drops, so a stale book is never recorded.

docs.title: Endpoints: depth on /public, trades on /market
docs.text:
Binance serves the USD-M streams on separate paths. Checked on 2026-11-10:

URL depth aggTrade wss://fstream.binance.com/stream?streams=… (legacy root) yes subscription accepted, nothing sent wss://fstream.binance.com/public/stream?streams=… yes — wss://fstream.binance.com/market/stream?streams=… — yes

A collector on the legacy root records books and silently no trade. The collector opens one connection to each path and keeps each alive with exponential backoff (Binance also closes every connection after 24 hours).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Offline tests (tests/unit/test_collect.py): the sequence rules (dropped, bridging, gap, snapshot older than the stream), the sampled features, hourly files and parts, and the full client against a local WebSocket server that serves depth on /public and trades on /market, with a scripted gap that must cause exactly one resync.
  • Live check (20 s, BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT, 2026-11-10): 2,446 trades, 365 depth events, 2 snapshots, 0 resyncs, 0 reconnects, no crossed sample; BTC spread one tick (0.014 bps).

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: The collector writes only under data/l2/ and takes no pipeline lock: the daily run never waits for it. It logs a status event every minute (messages, trades, samples, snapshots, resyncs, reconnects); a rising resync or reconnect count is the signal to look at the network. Files are not part of the R2 backup by default (they can be large); add data/l2/ to the backup if the propagator study needs months of books.

docs.title: What it enables
docs.text: A propagator model of impact (Bouchaud et al.) needs the mid-price response to each trade at fine resolution and the state of the book; with trades and 1-second books aligned on ts_ms, the response function and the lag structure can be estimated directly instead of through the same-side-run proxy of the impact exponent (§5). That study is future work.

docs.title: Literature watch
docs.text: Spec §2 asks for a search of arXiv ("order flow H0 crypto") and of the Rough Volatility Network list before starting, and again every month because the tested theory dates from 2026. The monthly search is automated: scripts/arxiv_watch.py runs in the literature workflow on the first day of each month and opens an issue listing the new papers. This page keeps what matters for the project.

docs.title: 2026-11-09 — check before the pre-registration
docs.text:
Searches: arXiv API over the last 400 days (scripts/arxiv_watch.py --days 400: order flow and crypto, roughness and crypto, order flow with impact and rough volatility, the authors of the theory) and web searches on signed order flow and long memory in crypto trades. The literature list of the Rough Volatility Network was not reviewed item by item (only its landing page was reached): to do by hand.

Result: no study tests the relations of the theory on crypto, or estimates H0 asset by asset. The claimed contribution (spec §2) stands. Closest work:

Paper Relation to this project Muhle-Karbe, Ouazzani Chahdi, Rosenbaum & Szymanski, A unified theory of order flow, market impact, and volatility (2026-01, v2 2026-02) the tested theory; equities, H0 ≈ 3/4 on average; the authors have posted nothing newer Multifractality and sample size influence on Bitcoin volatility patterns (Takaishi, 2025-11) and Multifractality in Bitcoin Realized Volatility: Implications for Rough Volatility Modelling (2025) multifractal analyses of Bitcoin realised volatility; the second argues that multifractality is incompatible with a monofractal rough model, one reason why H_σ has several estimators and the linearity of ζ(q) is a diagnostic Memory, Roughness, and Information Persistence in Financial Markets (2026-05) equities: H ≈ 0.06 for log realised variance across 115 S&P 500 stocks Kim & Hansen, The Quarter-Hour Effect (2026-07) periodic algorithmic trading in crypto futures: intraday seasonality finer than the hour of the week; relevant to the deseasonalisation robustness check Garcia Seuma, Where does the criticality live? (2026-07) early-warning signals across crypto-perpetual liquidation cascades; same microstructure, different question Caruso, Pricing and Calibration of Bitcoin Inverse Options via the Rough Bergomi Model (2026-08) option-implied roughness for Bitcoin; no order-flow estimate

Earlier crypto work measures the roughness of Bitcoin volatility (Rough volatility of Bitcoin, Takaishi) or the Hurst exponent of returns (Some stylized facts of the Bitcoin market), never the signed order flow together with volume, volatility and impact.

Next check: the literature workflow, every first of the month.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
One virtual machine is enough: the pipeline runs once a day, updates the rolling estimates and the dashboard. Target cost 0–5 € a month.

Component Choice Note Machine Oracle Cloud "Always Free", Arm Ampere A1 size for 2 cores / 12 GB; check the current free quota first Backups Cloudflare R2 via rclone scripts/backup.sh, weekly Monitoring Healthchecks.io ping each day; alert when missing HTTPS Caddy reverse proxy automatic certificates, rate limit module

Alternative: a laptop left on at night with the same docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Step by step on Oracle Cloud, with the set-up script of the machine (scripts/vm-setup.sh): Deploying on Oracle Cloud. In short:

git clone https://github.com/NIDHAL277/orderflow-scaling && cd orderflow-scaling
cp .env.example .env            # Healthchecks URL, hostnames, R2 credentials
mkdir -p data && sudo chown 1000 data
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
docker compose exec pipeline ofs status

Building behind a TLS-inspecting proxy or antivirus (one that re-signs HTTPS with its own root, such as Avast's "Web/Mail Shield"): the build's downloads fail with curl: (60) unable to get local issuer certificate. Export that root certificate as PEM and pass it as a build secret, which only the local image then trusts: docker build --secret id=extra_ca,src=root.pem -t orderflow-scaling:local . The proxy image takes the same secret: docker build -f docker/caddy.Dockerfile --secret id=extra_ca,src=root.pem -t ofs-caddy .

Rehearsing the CI job before a push, when developing on Windows or macOS: the workflow runs on Linux, where some things differ (worker processes are forked, not spawned; file names are case-sensitive). scripts/ci-rehearsal.sh runs the same steps in a container started from the local image, on a git bundle of the repository; its header gives the two commands. It found the hang described in an incident note.

docs.title: Daily run (ofs daily, cron 30 2-12 * * *)
docs.text:
1. 02:30 UTC: download yesterday's files; if absent, exit code 75 and retry every hour. Each run also replays the six days before (late files, failed downloads).
  2. Validation, reduction, update of the daily statistics. After Sunday's data, the files Binance re-published over the last 30 days are applied (ofs recheck), then the months that no run can change any more are folded into one file per statistic, pair and month (see "Monthly packs" below).
  3. Rolling 24-month estimates (confirmatory tests stay frozen on the frozen sample), then the live forecasts of every pair for the next 1, 5 and 22 days (data/forecast/live/{day}.parquet) and the live track record of past forecasts whose target is now complete (data/forecast/live_scored.parquet). Both need the protocol to allow the rolling estimates; a failure sets live_forecasts: false in the status and sends a fail ping, the data of the day being already saved. On the weekly recheck day, the change-point monitor of H0 runs too; pairs with an alarm in the latest block are listed in the status (changepoint_alarms) without failing the run.
  4. Healthchecks.io ping on success, fail ping otherwise (and at 12:xx UTC for files still absent, which become "missing").
  5. Sunday 04:00: backup of every derived table to R2 (scripts/backup.sh: daily statistics, estimates, tests, forecasts, manifest, validation, simulation, status, data quality, regime monitor, comparison of venues).

Exit codes: 0 done (later runs of the same day are no-ops), 75 waiting for Binance or another command writing the data, 1 failure.

Health (ofs status, GET /health, the dashboard) has three states. degraded: the last run reported a problem (blocked days, files still missing at 12:00 UTC, disk above 80 %, live forecasts failed); it comes first. stale: no problem reported, but the last verified day is more than 3 days old; Binance publishes a day later and the run retries until 12:30 UTC, so one or two days is normal, and older means that a run was missed or that the machine is stopped. ok otherwise. The age of the last verified day is always reported (data_lag_days).

One writer at a time: every command that writes the shared data (ingest, backfill, reduce, validate, recheck, history, estimate, test, daily, clean-temp) holds the operating-system lock data/status/pipeline.lock; a second writer exits at once with code 75 (cron retries it the next hour). The lock belongs to the open file, so a killed process never leaves it behind. status, quality, the API and the dashboard only read and never wait.

docs.title: L2 collector (optional, always on)
docs.text: docker compose --profile l2 up -d collector starts ofs collect-l2 for BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT and SOLUSDT (1-second books, 20 levels, every trade) into data/l2/. It takes no pipeline lock. Its status event every minute counts messages, snapshots, resyncs and reconnects; a growing resync count means a lossy network. See L2 collector.

docs.title: Backfill and data quality (O1)
docs.text:
ofs backfill --from 2024-11-01 --to 2026-10-31 --jobs 3   # resumable: done days are skipped
ofs quality  --from 2024-11-01 --to 2026-10-31            # exit 1 while O1 is not met

The backfill downloads chunk k+1 while chunk k is validated and reduced, and deletes each raw file once reduced, so at most two chunks (a few GB) of raw files are on disk. It is limited by bandwidth. Measured on 2026-11-09: 2024-11-01 for the 60 pairs and their perpetuals was 0.3 GB (volatile days are larger: the BTCUSDT perpetual alone was 46 MB on 2025-03-10), the connection gave 3.1 MB/s with 1 or 6 parallel downloads, and the day was reduced in 35 s with 4 processes. Reduced outputs take about 60 MB a day.

ofs quality writes data/quality/day_states.parquet (one row per pair, market and day) and data/quality/quality.parquet (days per state and coverage per pair). Every day of the window ends reduced, blocked (validation), or without a file: not_listed, delisted or suspended are explained; unexplained, not_reduced and not_attempted are not, and O1 requires none of them.

docs.title: Monthly packs
docs.text: The reduction writes one small file per statistic, pair and day; two years make about a million files, which a hard disk opens slowly and a backup uploads one by one. Once a month is out of reach of the daily replay and of the weekly recheck (35 days after its end), its per-day files are folded into one file per statistic, pair and month, {YYYY-MM}__pack.parquet (ADR 0016). The weekly run does it for the months that just closed; ofs compact does it for every closed month (resumable, holds the pipeline lock). Readers see the same rows either way; a day recomputed later (manual backfill, version bump) gets a per-day file that takes precedence until the next compaction folds it in.

docs.title: Results snapshot
docs.text:
ofs snapshot export                 # -> results-snapshot.zip (about 120 MB)
ofs snapshot fetch                  # latest release -> snapshot/ (or --source URL-or-file)
OFS_DATA_DIR=snapshot uv run streamlit run dashboards/app.py

The snapshot holds the tables the dashboard and the API read: tests, estimates without the bootstrap replicates, forecasts, simulation summaries, data quality, regime monitor, comparison of venues, manifest and status, with a manifest of sizes and SHA-256 checksums (snapshot.json). It holds no raw Binance file and no daily statistics. Attached to a release, it lets anyone browse the results without running the pipeline. fetch refuses unsafe paths, unlisted or missing files and checksum mismatches before it writes anything, and never overwrites a pipeline data directory. The dashboard recognises a snapshot and says so, instead of judging a pipeline that does not run there.

docs.title: Incidents
docs.text:
Incident Detection Action Daily file absent at 12:00 UTC status missing in the manifest replayed automatically by the next six daily runs; older gaps: ofs backfill --from D --to D; the dashboard shows the gap Wrong checksum M1 new download; two failures alert Binance format change M2 schema failure alert, fix the loader, add a regression test, replay Disk full alert at 80 % purge data/raw/, check deletion after reduction No run for days (machine stopped, cron down) health stale, data_lag_days above 3; no Healthchecks ping restart the stack; ofs backfill --from D --to D for days older than the six the daily run replays, then ofs daily Interrupted run (kill, reboot) *.tmp-* / *.part files ofs clean-temp --dry-run, then ofs clean-temp; rerun the command: done days are skipped Live forecasts failed status live_forecasts: false, fail ping read the live_forecasts_failed event in the log; the next daily run retries; a missing day of forecasts stays missing (forecasts are never made after the fact) Regression after deployment tests or dashboard OFS_IMAGE_TAG=<previous> docker compose up -d

Every real incident gets a three-line note in docs/incidents/: cause, fix, test added.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
The protocol prevents "finding" what one looks for: hypotheses frozen before the real data, a confirmation sample never touched while tuning, every variant published.

Step What Gate 0 config/preregistration.md committed (H1–H5, rule, estimators, grids, universe) tag prereg-v1 1 simulation study of every estimator: bias, RMSE, coverage O2, before step 0's tag 2 development sample (2024-11 → 2025-10): τ ranges, windows, gaps tag config-frozen 3 negative controls and power — 4 robustness: specification curve — 5 Holm over the three confirmatory tests; robustness descriptive —

The code enforces steps 0 and 2: ofs estimate refuses real data before prereg-v1, and the confirmation sample before config-frozen or if config/estimation.yaml changed since. In the production image the tags are baked at build time (ADR 0006).

The full text is config/preregistration.md.

docs.title: Commit ids in the results
docs.text:
Every row of the estimates, tests and forecast tables records code_version, the commit that computed it; the stamp ends in +dirty when tracked files had uncommitted changes, and no result row has it. Before the first push to GitHub (18 November 2026) the history was rewritten once, only to replace the author email with GitHub's private address: the files, dates and messages of every commit are unchanged, but every commit id changed. The results were computed earlier, so they record the earlier ids:

code_version in the results Public commit Results e88fe171072d e01f7d96acd9, tag config-frozen confirmation estimates and tests, forecast confirmation tests, estimates history 801063739473 f14b95e57c3b development estimates, forecast development tests b54080239763 9e65d28dd17e development tests 2bc09c381596 d40500f53f07 rolling estimates

The confirmatory results were therefore computed at the commit tagged config-frozen itself, with no uncommitted change.

docs.title: Timeline (12 weeks, ~15 h a week)
docs.text:
Phase Weeks Gate P0 Framing S1 CI green, protocol written P1 Ingestion and reduction S2–S3 statistics = naive computation P2 Simulation and estimators S4–S5 O2 met, tag prereg-v1 P3 Full universe, development S6–S7 tag config-frozen P4 Confirmation and tests S8–S9 H1–H5 decided P5 Production S10 daily pipeline online P6 Report and dissemination S11–S12 report submitted, README ready

More than two weeks late at the end of S7: cut the scope to 20 spot pairs and H1, H2 only.

docs.title: Other venues: Bybit and OKX (exploratory)
docs.text: Every confirmatory result of this project comes from one exchange. Crypto order flow is split across venues, and the persistence H0 measured on Binance need not be that of the market: the paper lists this among its limitations. This page measures how much the answer depends on the venue, on a small scale and outside the frozen protocol.

docs.title: What is compared
docs.text:
For the five most liquid pairs, spot and linear perpetual, over the same days:

  • Binance: the daily statistics of the main pipeline.
  • Bybit and OKX: the daily trade files of their public archives (data sources), reduced by the same code into folders of their own (data/venues/bybit, data/venues/okx), so the venues never mix.

The exponent is the principal H0 estimator of the study (mixed fractional model on the flow centred day by day in proportion to volume), fitted on the days present on every venue. The interval is a moving-block bootstrap over days, with the same resamples on each venue.

Four differences from the confirmatory tests, to keep in mind when reading:

  1. Descriptive. No hypothesis was registered for this comparison and no decision rule applies; the protocol guard treats it like the rolling estimates.
  2. Intervals not calibrated. The confirmatory intervals are widened by a factor fixed in the simulation study; these are raw, on one month, so they are narrow.
  3. Weaker integrity checks. Neither archive publishes checksums. A Bybit file counts when its size is the announced one and its gzip stream decompresses to the end; an OKX file when the CRC of its zip member is right. The reduction's own controls then apply.
  4. Different conventions, aligned here. Both archives list every fill, Binance one row per taker order and price: fills with the same time, side and price are merged. OKX cuts its daily files at midnight in Hong Kong (16:00 UTC), so each UTC day is rebuilt from two files; its perpetual sizes are in contracts, a constant factor on which no scaling exponent depends.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Written for the run of 2026-11-16 (October 2026, five pairs).

  • Perpetuals: the venue matters little. The three exchanges give a persistence between 0.57 and 0.69 for every pair. Bybit differs from Binance by a few thousandths on average and by less than 0.04 on any pair; OKX is lower than Binance by about 0.03 on average and 0.07 at most. The persistence near 0.6 measured on Binance's perpetuals is not a feature of Binance.
  • Spot: noisier, without a direction. Bybit and OKX trade between two and six times less than Binance on these pairs. OKX differs from Binance by 0.07 at most, above on some pairs and below on others; Bybit is higher on two pairs, by 0.16, and not identified on a third. On a thin market one month is short.
  • On perpetuals the differences between venues, a few hundredths, are small next to the gap between spot and perpetuals on Binance (about 0.1), which the confirmatory tests measure (H5).
  • A month and five pairs describe; they do not test.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
uv run ofs venues --to 2026-10-31 --days 30 --publish

About 600 files (1 to 15 MB each) are downloaded, reduced and deleted; the daily statistics stay under data/venues/, so a second run only recomputes the table. --venue bybit or --venue okx selects one archive, --symbol other pairs, --market spot or --market um one market.

docs.title: ADR 0001 — Record architecture decisions
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: the project is reviewed by quantitative researchers; choices that change a number must be traceable.

Decision: every non-obvious technical or statistical choice gets a short record here: context, decision, consequences. Statistical choices that affect the confirmatory tests are also written in config/preregistration.md before the tag prereg-v1.

Consequences: a deviation after the tag needs both a new ADR and an entry in the report's "Deviations from protocol".

docs.title: ADR 0002 — Per-day outputs versioned in the file name
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: every stage must be idempotent and replayable for one pair and one day; a change of algorithm or configuration must recompute exactly what depends on it.

Decision: per-day outputs are written as {day}__v{version}.parquet in symbol=/market=/month= partitions, atomically (temporary file + rename). The version is {stage version}.{hash of the configuration fragment the stage reads}; stage versions are bumped by hand in ofs.versioning.STAGE_VERSIONS. A stage skips a day whose file with the current version exists and replaces other versions of that day.

Consequences: re-running is free; editing a grid in config/ recomputes pass 2 but not pass 1 (which would need raw trades again). Results carry the git commit (code_version) and the full configuration hash (config_version).

docs.title: ADR 0003 — Causal hour-of-week profile
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: crypto has a strong weekly seasonality; every series is divided by its mean profile per hour of the week (168 cells) before estimation (spec §5.1). A profile computed on the whole sample would make daily updates rewrite all past statistics.

Decision: pass 1 stores per-day partial sums per cell (count, sum of V, sum of F²); the profile used for day d is computed on the trailing 84 days ending at d (12 observations per cell). Volume is divided by its mean profile, signed flow by its root-mean-square profile, both normalised to mean one. For the first week of a series, the first 7 available days are used (a documented look-ahead of at most 6 days).

Consequences: daily statistics never change once written; the profile adapts slowly to regime changes. The specification curve includes a variant without deseasonalisation.

docs.title: ADR 0004 — Additive daily statistics and the synchronized bootstrap
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: the bootstrap needs 999 re-estimations of every exponent for every pair, with the same resampled days for all pairs, without re-reading trades.

Decision: every estimator consumes per-day sums (increments, squares, ACF sums, moment sums, binned runs). Increments of a daily series (daily RV) are attached to their start day, so they are additive too. A bootstrap replicate is a vector of day counts w_b drawn once per sample by a stationary bootstrap (mean block 7 days) and applied to every pair: fit(w_b @ daily_matrix). The Whittle estimator, which needs a contiguous series, re-estimates on the block-resampled series and drops increments across block joins.

Consequences: the bootstrap is a matrix product plus a fit; the cross-sectional correlation of estimation errors between cryptos is preserved; replicates and day indices are stored with the estimates for audit.

docs.title: ADR 0005 — Volatility: extraday horizon; principal estimator decided by simulation
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08). The full simulation study then made Whittle the principal estimator, a deviation from the rule recorded as D1 (2026-11-10, config/deviations.md).

Context: the paper states the volatility prediction 2H0 − 3/2 for the extraday volatility (Remark 4.2) and quotes intraday estimates near 0.25 as a different object. Preliminary simulations of rough Bergomi show that GJR moments on daily RV are biased upward near zero (≈ +0.13 to +0.19 for H ∈ {0.05, 0.1}) because daily integration smooths the path, while the Whittle estimator of Fukasawa, Takabatake & Westphal stays close.

Decision: daily horizon primary; intraday descriptive. The principal estimator follows the rule of config/preregistration.md §4.1, applied to the full simulation study before the tag prereg-v1; both estimators are always computed and bootstrapped. GJR lags extend to 50 days (the bias falls with longer lags).

Consequences: H2 may be "not decided" if neither estimator is reliable near zero; the report then states the sample size that would be needed.

docs.title: ADR 0006 — Protocol state baked into the production image
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: ofs.protocol checks the git tags prereg-v1 and config-frozen and that config/estimation.yaml is unchanged since config-frozen. The production image has no .git directory.

Decision: the release workflow passes, as build arguments, the protocol tags present (OFS_PROTOCOL_TAGS) and the SHA-256 of config/estimation.yaml at config-frozen (OFS_FROZEN_CONFIG_SHA256); the guard accepts them in place of git and compares the hash with the configuration shipped in the image. OFS_CODE_VERSION carries the commit.

Consequences: the daily rolling estimates run in production only from images built after prereg-v1; an image whose configuration drifted from the frozen one refuses confirmatory runs.

docs.title: ADR 0007 — Daily files for the backfill, chunked deletion
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: Binance publishes monthly aggTrades files for historical catch-up, but a liquid pair's monthly file holds tens of millions of trades, beyond the 8 GB memory budget once parsed; downloading 24 months for 60 pairs before reducing would also need hundreds of GB of disk.

Decision: the backfill uses daily files, processed in chunks of 7 days: download (8 in parallel), validate, pass 1, delete the raw file, then pass 2 of the chunk. (pair, market) groups run in parallel processes (--jobs).

Consequences: disk use stays at a few GB; memory peaks at one day of the largest pair (< 1 GB for BTCUSDT); more HTTP requests, absorbed by the CDN.

docs.title: ADR 0008 — H0: uncentred variances, 1/τ weights, identification of the fractional part
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08). Point (1) and the negative control amended by ADR 0015 (deviations D3, D4): on real data the daily imbalance rides on clustered activity, so the flow is now centred day by day in proportion to volume and the fit models the centring exactly. Points (2) and (3) stand.

Context: three problems found in simulation and property tests.

  1. Subtracting the sample mean of overlapping increments biases the variance down at large τ under long memory (≈ −0.05 on H at H = 0.9).
  2. With equal weights in log space the 4-hour points, estimated from few independent increments, dominate the curvature: the standard deviation of Ĥ0 doubles.
  3. On Brownian data (shuffled signs) the mixed model is flat in H and the fit drifts to a bound (H ≈ 1).

Decision: (1) the principal uses uncentred mean squared increments: the model has no drift and the daily net imbalance of the real flow is part of its long memory; (2) weighted NLS with weights ∝ 1/τ, the inverse variance of log V̂(τ) under the Brownian null (the "weighted" fit of spec §5.2); (3) the fractional component is retained only if, at the largest τ, it explains more than twice the sampling error of the variance there (2·sqrt(4m/3n), floor 5 %); otherwise H0 = 1/2. The shuffled-sign control removes each day's mean increment (the permutation keeps the day's imbalance, a drift) and corrects the shrinkage this causes exactly.

Consequences: in simulation (12 days), |bias| ≤ 0.02 for H0 ∈ [0.6, 0.9] with noise/signal up to 2, and shuffled signs give 0.49–0.52.

docs.title: ADR 0009 — OHLC check against klines: robust to one-tick feed differences
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-08)

Context: spec §6.4 blocks a day when the OHLC rebuilt from aggTrades differs from the 1-minute klines by more than 0.01 %. On real files, spot matches exactly (deviation 0), but USD-M klines include trades absent from aggTrades (1-5 % extra volume in some minutes). On the STRKUSDT perpetual (price about 0.04, tick 0.00001), 6 minute opens and 1 minute low of 2026-11-05 differed by 1-2 ticks, i.e. 0.025-0.05 %, and the whole day was blocked.

The likely cause is RPI (Retail Price Improvement) orders on Binance futures: their fills would be counted in the klines but not published in aggTrades. Bybit's archive flags such fills in an RPI column. Binance documentation does not confirm this, so it stays a hypothesis. It does not change the decision below.

Decision: a day fails if a kline minute has no aggTrades, if any minute is off by more than 1 % (gross error), or if more than 0.5 % of the minutes are off by more than max(0.01 %, 2 ticks), the tick being the smallest step between the day's distinct trade prices. Every deviation is reported in the validation detail. Setting ohlc_tolerance_ticks: 0 and max_ohlc_bad_minute_fraction: 0 restores the literal rule.

Consequences: reconstruction errors (wrong time unit, wrong day, truncated file, corrupted prices) are still caught; the structural one- or two-tick difference of the futures feed no longer drops perpetual days needed by H5.

Amendment (2026-11-09, validation stage version 2): on the first week of the real backfill, the NEIROUSDT perpetual of 2024-11-07 (1.97 M trades) was blocked: 8 of 1440 minutes had a kline open 3 to 10 ticks away from the first trade of the minute. In all 77 minutes where the kline open differs from the first trade, it equals the last trade of the previous minute, and the first trade of the minute comes 0 to 274 ms after the boundary; closes match in every minute and the kline high/low always contain the aggTrades range. This is a convention of the USD-M klines at the minute boundary, not a data error. The open is now compared with the first trade of the minute and with the last trade before it; the closer one counts. With this rule the day has 1 minute beyond tolerance and passes; a wrong open (neither price) still counts as a deviation.

docs.title: ADR 0010 — Daily catch-up window and application of re-published files
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-09)

Context: spec §11.4 asks to replay a day whose file was still absent at 12:00 UTC, and §6.4 to apply the correction files published by Binance. The daily run processed yesterday only, so a late file was never picked up. Binance Vision has no updates folder: a corrected file replaces the old one at the same URL with a new .CHECKSUM, and ofs ingest --recheck downloaded it again but left the statistics computed from the old file in place (the day was already reduced, so it was skipped).

Decision:

  • Each daily run processes a window of catchup_days (7) ending yesterday. Days already reduced cost one file-existence check; missing and error days are attempted again.
  • ofs recheck --from --to (and the daily run after the recheck_weekday, over the last recheck_days) compares the published checksums with the manifest. For each changed pair-day it deletes the windows, statistics and validation report of that day, downloads both files again, validates and reduces the day, and recomputes pass 2 of the days whose seasonal profile includes it (the trailing 84 days after it, the first week before it).

Consequences: a late or corrected file reaches the statistics without manual work. A full recheck of the 24-month window (about 170 000 checksum requests) is run by hand before the configuration is frozen for the confirmation sample.

docs.title: ADR 0011 — Five-year daily-volatility history as a separate sample
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-09)

Context: spec §4 includes "up to 5 years for the daily volatility when the history exists". A 12-month sample gives about 365 daily observations for lags up to 50 days, the weakest point of H2 (spec §13). Trades are only collected for the 24-month window, but Binance publishes monthly 1-minute klines for every listed month.

Decision:

  • ofs history downloads the monthly 1-minute klines of 2021-11 → 2026-10 (spot and perpetual, renames followed month by month: a rename month has one file per symbol) and keeps, per UTC day, the 5-minute RV and the TSRV (daily_stats/rv_history, one file per pair, market and month). Days with less than 95 % of their minutes or without any trade are left out (Binance publishes flat klines for a few days after a perpetual stops).
  • The history sample runs the daily H_σ estimators only, variant daily_5y, with its own synchronized block bootstrap over the five years. Because it includes the confirmation year, it needs the config-frozen tag like the confirmation sample.
  • Its estimates join the specification curve of H2 against Ĥ0 of the sample. The tests themselves keep the four exponents estimated on the same data (spec §2, claim 1).

Consequences: a more precise daily H_σ is reported as robustness without changing the confirmatory tests. The pairing of bootstrap replicates across the two samples treats their errors as independent, which the report states next to the variant.

docs.title: ADR 0012 — Trade-id continuity: block missing rows, not unpublished fills
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-09)

Context: spec §6.4 asks for strictly increasing ids and first/last continuity, every hole logged. The first rule blocked a day above 0.1 % of missing trade ids. Measured on the real files: spot has no hole at all; USD-M perpetuals miss short runs of trade ids (median 1 id, longest 25) on 83 % of days, 0.01-0.02 % of the ids in the first half of 2025 and 0.12 % in August 2025, 0.21 % on an ordinary day of October 2025 and 0.23-0.32 % on the 2025-10-10 liquidation cascade (concentrated in its hour). Over the 2 479 pair-days validated so far, and on these days, the aggTrade ids are always consecutive. The missing trade ids are fills that are never published in the public trade feed (likely the RPI orders of ADR 0009, which the klines include): the files are complete. The 0.1 % rule would have blocked most perpetual days from mid-2025 and kept their raw files (about 250 GB).

Decision: the day is blocked when an aggTrade row is missing (a gap in agg_trade_id), when one run of more than 1000 consecutive trade ids is missing (a lost chunk), when more than 2 % of the trade ids are missing, or when ids overlap (last < first, negative gaps). Every gap is still logged with its count and the longest run. Validation stage version 3.

Consequences: complete perpetual files pass; a file that loses rows is still blocked by the aggTrade ids, and a truncated day by the OHLC check (kline minutes without trades). The share of unpublished trade ids is kept in the validation report for each day.

docs.title: ADR 0013 — Forecasting extension: exact rough predictor, model-based levels
docs.text:
Status: accepted (2026-11-10)
